articles.title: Track II diplomacy: Time to rethink Nepal’s diaspora
articles.summary:
‘Supreme organic investor’ sounds more like a high-grade crop fertiliser. Rather it is a prestigious status for the Nepali Diaspora community under the National Commitment. The 18-point governing plan was released by Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s Cabinet weeks after assuming office. A promising gesture of annual investment bonds, guaranteed ancestral property, a path to the ballot, and protection and continuity of citizenship were listed in the commitment.

The instinct is understandable, as remittances equal roughly a quarter of Nepal’s GDP—among the highest ratios in the world. More than 2.1 million Nepalis live outside the country, and closer to 4.5 million counting people of Nepali descent. The Non-Resident Nepali Association reaches into almost 90 countries. A reforming government is eager to translate patriotic feeling into hard capital, and a diaspora seated on decades of savings is a reasonable place to look at. But this reflects a consistent pattern of misunderstanding of what diaspora is actually worth and how to mobilise it for statecraft.

Nepal’s first integrated foreign policy adopted in 2020 explicitly lists ‘Track II diplomacy’ among the country’s instruments of statecraft. The phrase sits in the doctrine, unused like a treadmill in a spare room. American diplomat Joseph Montville coined the term ‘Track II diplomacy’ for the low-key, unofficial work by which private citizens and other non-state actors pry open channels that formal Track I diplomacy cannot. Nepal maintains roughly 40 missions for a diaspora spread across more than twice as many countries. This is where Track II diplomacy naturally steps in.

Diaspora networks do not replace state diplomacy. They lower the cost of access and improve the odds. For a country that cannot afford access at all, Nepal is badly in need of one.

Two decades ago, India faced the same issue: A constitution that would not permit dual citizenship and a diaspora that wanted one. Delhi’s answer was to invent a substitute, the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, codified in the Citizenship Act. But its smarter move came in 2016 when the diaspora portfolio was folded into the Ministry of External Affairs, and diaspora work stopped being classified as welfare and became part of foreign policy.

Nepal does not need the constitution to plot the move. India could not grant dual citizenship either, so it built a formidable institution to house it where foreign policy is mandated. Nepal has the same constraint, and half the answer already exists: A Labour Migration and Diaspora Coordination Division sitting well within the foreign ministry. It needs coordination rather than convening.

Ireland managed to get the diaspora relationship right but the politics wrong. It lets the grandchild of an Irish-born citizen claim dual citizenship, keeping the second and third generations legally attached rather than merely sentimental. Since 2004, its Emigrant Support Programme has spent over 170 million euro funding some 600 Irish organisations abroad, paying into the diaspora’s own institutions. Dublin promised a referendum on presidential voting rights in 2013 and never held one. Kathmandu has made the same promise. Ireland shows the relationship can be built regardless. It did not wait for the franchise, and neither should Nepal.

Armenia is a cautionary tale. It got the law right with a 2005 referendum lifting the constitutional ban on dual citizenship and a 2007 amendment to the Law on Citizenship. But it suffered institutionally. The Ministry of Diaspora, established in 2008, concluded disastrously 11 years later. The Armenian journal EVN Report’s assessment mentions it as a bureaucratic fiefdom that cold-shouldered investors without connections, duplicated the foreign ministry and forfeited the trust of the people it served. Its replacement is small by design; an office under the prime minister mandated to map diaspora expertise. The technology sector has since reached roughly 7 percent of GDP on that expertise. The lesson is that the wrong kind of diaspora institution shadows the foreign ministry and spends down trust a generation in the making. This brings us back to the Brain Gain Centre that sits under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Reviving it as a bigger registry would repeat Yerevan’s mistake. It certainly needs a different stance, drawing on examples from the three countries above.

First, Nepal needs to keep the diaspora establishment small, accountable and housed inside the foreign ministry. Second, it needs to map the diaspora by institution and jurisdiction rather than by name and profession. This allows the state to know who sits where, on which board and how to revise lobbying. Lastly, we could borrow Dublin’s patience: build the relationship and let it percolate while the constitutional questions follow, because none of this waits on an amendment, a referendum, or a two-thirds majority.

Track II advises; it certainly does not govern. The Diaspora Community is powerful to influence and inform Nepal’s positions, not to vote on them. That is also why it fits the constitution rather than straining it. The charter binds the state to an independent, non-aligned foreign policy in the national interest and says nothing about who may help pursue one. Three nations have paid for three distinct lessons along the way.

The takeaways are entirely free. But whether Nepal learns from these nations and builds a real strategy is entirely up to Kathmandu. If executed correctly, it could yield actual leverage for the state. Executed incorrectly, the Supreme Organic Investor remains nothing more than the expensive fertiliser it sounds like.

articles.title: End attacks against health workers, keep health services running
articles.summary:
On Saturday, Dr Pramod Ram, a doctor at Narayani Hospital in Birgunj, was assaulted by relatives of a 45-year-old patient who died while undergoing treatment in the hospital’s emergency ward. The attackers also vandalised hospital property and threatened other health workers. The incident prompted the hospital to suspend services, with all staff resigning en masse in protest.

The Nepal Medical Association, an umbrella organisation of medical and dental doctors, supported the protest by halting all non-emergency health services nationwide. While the strike was withdrawn on Wednesday evening, hundreds of thousands of patients were already deprived of medical care on Tuesday and Wednesday. Patients ultimately bear the brunt of such disruptions. Those who reached hospitals and health centres after travelling long distances are forced to return without treatment. People from low-income backgrounds, many of whom have to take loans or borrow money even to afford medical expenses, are hit the hardest.

Ceasing health services, therefore, cannot be justified under any circumstances. Hundreds of thousands of patients cannot be penalised for the wrongdoing of a few individuals. Moreover, suspending health services is illegal. The Health Service Act categorically recognises medical services as essential services that cannot be halted. Similarly, the Public Health Service Act states that no citizen shall be deprived of health services. By suspending essential services, the association has not only increased the hardships faced by patients but has also challenged the legal provisions governing healthcare delivery.

This, however, does not mean that attacks and threats against doctors and health workers should be overlooked. Physical assaults on medical professionals are criminal acts that require immediate legal action. The fact that around 90 incidents of physical attacks and assaults against health workers have taken place within a period of just 10 months highlights the urgency of the issue and demands swift intervention.

Ensuring proper security arrangements in the health sector must be a top priority for the government. Doctors and health workers are there to save and treat patients, not to harm them. Patients and their relatives, therefore, need to have faith in them. However, negligence on the part of doctors and health workers cannot be ruled out. There are bodies responsible for investigating such cases and taking appropriate action. Manhandling doctors and health workers is not the solution. In several instances, the compulsion for junior staff to handle complicated cases, coupled with inadequate resources, has led to unwanted treatment outcomes. It is the state that needs to address these shortcomings.

Medical facilities should be a safe space for doctors and health workers to work, while patients also have the right to receive proper treatment. Both can go hand in hand. Ensuring uninterrupted health services, strengthening security, and holding attackers accountable are of utmost importance. The situation in which health professionals have to work in constant fear, and health services are disrupted under any pretext, should end once and for all.

articles.title: Where diversity becomes national identity
articles.summary:
My visits to the Swiss Parliament in Bern over recent years left me with many unforgettable impressions, but none stood out more than the symbolism enshrined beneath its grand central dome. Standing in that historic hall, one looks not merely at classical architecture, but at the very visual soul of a constitutional democracy.

At the centre of the dome stand the Three Confederates, recalling the historic 1291 oath that founded the Swiss Confederation. Flanking them are four armed figures representing Switzerland’s national languages: German, French, Italian, and Romansh. Surrounding this central assembly are the official coats of arms, flags, and distinctive emblems of all twenty-six Swiss cantons, woven directly into the stained glass and stonework.

What makes this display extraordinary is that architecture mirrors constitutional reality. The cantonal coats of arms and regional flags prominently decorating the parliamentary walls send an unmistakable message that the federal state derives its identity directly from the sovereignty, dignity, and equality of its constituent parts. Over one hundred thousand visitors, ranging from local students to foreign dignitaries, tour these historic halls every year. They do not visit merely to admire nineteenth-century craft, but to observe how a country transformed vast geographic, linguistic, and cultural diversity into one of the world’s most stable and admired democracies.

This constitutional equality is reflected directly in how the Swiss Parliament operates day to day. The Federal Assembly consists of two chambers operating on strictly equal footing in all legislative aspects: the National Council, with two hundred members representing the general public, and the Council of States, with forty-six members representing the cantons with two seats per full canton and one seat per half-canton.

Neither house is superior to the other, meaning every piece of legislation must pass both chambers in identical form before becoming law. Furthermore, every year both houses convene together as the United Federal Assembly to elect the President of the Confederation for a one-year term and to appoint or confirm the seven-member executive cabinet known as the Federal Council.

Throughout these legislative proceedings, institutional multilingualism allows members to speak freely in their native languages during debates supported by real-time translation, ensuring that language is never a barrier to equal political participation. Despite covering just forty-one thousand square kilometres; roughly the size of Nepal’s Karnali Province; Switzerland empowers twenty-six cantons, each possessing its own constitution, parliament, government, and deep local identity.

As Switzerland celebrates its National Day on the first of August; an occasion that coincides with the milestone seventieth anniversary of diplomatic relations between Switzerland and Nepal; it offers a timely moment for reflection. Unlike national celebrations centered on military parades or central state authority, Swiss National Day is celebrated from the ground up. Across the country, communities gather around hilltop bonfires, lantern processions, parish bells, and local music. Every canton celebrates in its own distinct way, reflecting regional customs, dialects, and cuisine while sharing a single national identity.

Swiss constitutional scholar Professor Eva Maria Belser of the Institute of Federalism describes Switzerland as a ‘willensnation’, or a ‘nation of will’. It is bound together not by a single ethnicity, language, or religion, but by the conscious decision of its citizens to coexist under shared democratic institutions.

In this framework, diversity is not viewed as an administrative challenge to be managed from the capital, but as the foundational pillar of the state itself. Power in Switzerland is guided by the principle of subsidiarity, meaning public tasks are handled by the lowest possible administrative level; communes and cantons and only elevated to the federal level when strictly necessary. Cantons hold primary authority over education, local administration, culture, and policing.

As Swiss Ambassador to Nepal, Dr Danielle Meuwly, noted during a tour of the parliament, national unity does not require cultural uniformity; it requires everyday institutional practice that makes every community feel true ownership of the nation.

Like Switzerland, Nepal possesses extraordinary cultural and geography-driven richness. With more than one hundred and twenty languages spoken across the Himal, Hills, and Tarai regions, Nepal’s Constitution rightly recognises all mother tongues as national languages. Yet recognition on paper remains incomplete unless actively supported through provincial legislation, public administration, cultural academies, and local education policies. Languages and local heritages survive when they are actively used, taught, published, and celebrated in public life.

This is where Nepal’s seven provinces play a crucial constitutional role that is often underestimated. Provinces are not mere administrative divisions for budget allocation or public expenditure; they are constitutional spaces where local cultures receive formal institutional backing and protection. Through these provincial structures, citizens see their regional identity reflected directly in governance.

For instance, Koshi Province provides institutional space for Kirat, Limbu, and Rai traditions, Madhesh promotes Maithili, Bhojpuri, and Tharu heritage, Bagmati strengthens Nepal Bhasa and Tamang, Gandaki honors Gurung, Magar, and Himalayan cultures, Lumbini preserves Tharu, Awadhi, and Magar traditions, Karnali upholds Khas civilization, and Sudurpashchim nurtures Doteli and Rana Tharu heritage. Such provincial initiatives allow citizens across all regions to recognize themselves within the national identity.

A recent example illustrates this point vividly. During the budget discussions of the Bagmati Provincial Assembly, Finance and Development Committee Chair Nuraj Bajracharya posed a question in Newa, and Finance Minister Prabhat Tamang replied in Tamang. The video quickly spread across social media, demonstrating how provincial institutions can become meaningful platforms for recognising Nepal's linguistic diversity in public life.

Building mature institutions takes patience and time. Switzerland’s federal system has evolved through one hundred and seventy-eight years of modern constitutional practice and seven centuries of confederate history. Nepal’s federal journey, by contrast, is still in its first decade. Rather than questioning provincial structures because they are evolving, our focus should remain on making them stronger, more capable, more accountable, and more responsive so they can fulfill the constitutional purpose for which they were created.

A walk through Bern reveals a capital city that is impeccably organized and clean, where the turquoise Aare River flows crystal-clear through the city center. Seeing such environmental care inevitably makes one reflect on our own Bagmati, reminding us that federalism and local governance must also extend to restoring and cherishing our natural heritage.

Standing beneath the dome of the Federal Palace in Bern and seeing the coats of arms and flags of every canton displayed alongside federal symbols offers a profound insight into democratic harmony. However, every country carries its own unique history, political culture, social reality, and governance needs. Pointing to the Swiss model does not mean Nepal must blindly copy or import another nation's practices into our own context. What works on the slopes of the Alps cannot simply be transplanted onto the slopes of the Himalayas without thoughtful local adaptation.

Instead, the true value of observing Switzerland lies in the universal principle it demonstrates: federalism succeeds when institutional practice matches constitutional promises, ensuring every community feels valued.

As we join in celebrating Swiss National Day and mark seventy years of enduring friendship between Nepal and Switzerland, the core message is one of optimism and pride. Nepal’s immense diversity is not a weakness to be overcome, but our greatest national strength.

By continually strengthening our federal institutions, empowering our provinces, and ensuring every community feels respected within our shared national home, Nepal can continue to forge its own proud, inclusive, and resilient federal republic democratic tradition. On this joyous occasion of Swiss National Day, I extend my warmest greetings and best wishes to the people and government of Switzerland. May the enduring friendship between Nepal and Switzerland grow ever stronger.

articles.title: Booktalk: In search of the perfect note
articles.summary:
Salina BK is a Nepali singer who first came into the national spotlight through ‘Nepal Idol’ and ‘Nepal Star’. Known for her powerful vocals and expressive performances, she has since continued her musical journey through live concerts while pursuing a Master's degree in Music, deepening her understanding of Indian classical traditions.

The Post's Shrinkhala Chand Thakuri sat with BK to talk about lifelong learning, finding inspiration, the role of emotion in music, and the books, films and musical traditions that continue to shape her as an artist.

What has been occupying your mind lately in terms of music?

Musically, I've been spending a lot of time exploring different raags and trying to understand their depth and emotional expression. I'm also constantly working on improving my understanding of classical music because I believe learning never stops.

Do you actively seek inspiration, or do you wait for it to find you?

I don't think inspiration comes only by waiting. The more you learn, observe and keep yourself connected to music, the more inspiration naturally finds its way to you.

Are you a regular reader? What kind of books do you naturally gravitate towards?

I would say I am more of a listener. But whenever I do read, I naturally gravitate towards books related to music, musicians and the art of learning music.

When you're preparing a song, what do you focus on first—the lyrics, the melody or the emotion?

For me, it always begins with emotion. Once I understand what the song is trying to make people feel, the lyrics and melody naturally come together to express that emotion.

Outside of singing, what have you been reading, watching or listening to recently?

Lately, I have been listening to a lot of classical music, especially different raags and traditional compositions. Since I'm pursuing my Master's in Music, most of my time outside singing also goes into studying and understanding music from different perspectives.

What's one song you wish you had written yourself?

Honestly, I do not look back and wish I had written someone else's song. I'd rather hope that one day people will say they wish they had written one of my songs.

Has your relationship with music changed since ‘Nepal Idol’ and ‘Nepal Star’?

Absolutely. Those experiences helped me understand where I stand as an artist and showed me how much more there is to learn. They gave me clarity about the direction I want to take and how I need to keep growing as a musician.

If you weren't a singer, what creative field do you think you'd have ended up in?

Honestly, I've never really imagined myself doing anything other than music. This is what I've loved and worked towards for as long as I can remember, so it's difficult for me to picture myself in any other creative field.

Salina BK's book recommendations

Author: Hermann Hesse

Publisher: S. Fischer

This is a philosophical novel about a man's quest for spiritual enlightenment. I love its portrayal of a seeker's journey towards self-discovery and inner peace.

The Seven Spiritual Laws of SuccessAuthor: Deepak ChopraYear: 1994Publisher: Amber-Allen Publishing

Its simple yet powerful principles show how inner awareness, purposeful action and harmony with life can lead to personal fulfilment and lasting success.

Autobiography of a YogiAuthor: Paramahansa YoganandaYear: 1946Publisher: Philosophical Library

Yogananda’s spiritual memoir details his spiritual journey. It offers a beautiful perspective on self-realisation and the search for a deeper understanding of life.

The Alchemist

Author: Paulo Coelho

Publisher: Rocco

Its inspiring story about following one’s dreams and listening to one’s heart reminds me that the journey towards a goal can be as meaningful as the destination.

The Power of NowAuthor: Eckhart TolleYear: 1997Publisher: Namaste Publishing

Its emphasis on living fully in the present moment has helped me understand how inner peace begins by letting go of unnecessary worries about the past and future.

Salina BK's music recommendations

Pokhiyera Ghamko JhulkoSinger: Narayan Gopal

Narayan Gopal's voice carries an unmatched warmth and sincerity. Every time I listen to this song, I discover a new emotion hidden within its melody.

Tan Man BachanleSinger: Bhakta Raj Acharya

This song is a beautiful expression of devotion. Bhakta Raj Acharya's honesty and depth of feeling remind me of the emotional power that music can hold.

Timra Pau HarumaSinger: Tara Devi

Tara Devi's voice has a rare grace and purity. This song is timeless, and I admire the way it expresses love and reverence with such simplicity.

Eklai BasdaSinger: Arun Thapa

Arun Thapa had an extraordinary ability to make loneliness sound beautiful. This song always takes me inward and reminds me how powerful honest music can be.

Tada Tada Januchha SathiSinger: Prem Dhoj Pradhan

This is one of those songs that stays with you long after it ends. Its melody and sense of longing capture a feeling that words alone cannot express.

articles.title: Movie review: The price of artistic immortality
articles.summary:
A protagonist’s moral ambiguity is rarely announced in a celebratory, character-driven story. However, such is the creative risk taken by the makers of ‘Kokuho’ and it is the very quality that defines the film’s artistic triumph.

The film opens with the New Year’s celebration hosted by the leader of a yakuza gang. There, his son, Kikuo performs Kabuki; a traditional Japanese theatre in which onnagata (male actors who specialise in female roles) occupy a revered place. Among the audience is Hanjiro Hanai, regarded as Osaka’s greatest Kabuki actor, who is immediately captivated by the fourteen-year-old’s talent.

Soon after, the child witnesses his father’s murder. Although the story initially appears to be steering toward revenge, it swiftly pivots into the demanding and disciplined world of Kabuki, where Kikuo is taken under Hanjiro’s guidance along with his own biological son Shunshuke.

Kabuki ultimately replaces vengeance for Kikuo. Rather than fighting fire with fire, he channels his grief toward Kabuki as the only choice for survival and refuge. But along the way, it consumes every part of his identity, making it a matter of esteem, then eventually an irresistible pride.

With Shunshuke’s and Kikuo’s journeys existing with equal depths of characterisation and narrative arc, the audience is made to empathise, question, relate, resist, all while the story moves with a memorable flow.

Spanning over five decades of timeline, ‘Kokuho’ follows their relentless pursuit of artistic greatness. Within this, it explores the tradition of onnagata, born from the historical exclusion of women on stage. Eventually, through the performers’ embodiment of femininity, the film reveals a devotion to art along with the defiance of gender norms.

Kikuo’s one particular recurring vision drives the film’s exploration of moral ambiguity. A dark expanse filled with falling white fragments and scattered sparks of light shows a mind caught between innocence and obsession. Kikuo’s battle becomes the one with himself and his desire to become indispensable to Kabuki, rather than the one against the men who killed his father.

Along this depiction, ‘Kokuho’ leaves a cinematic mark with its cinematography and masterful use of light and colour. The interplay of light and shadow, bright and muted colours, warm and cool texture surely heightens the film’s aesthetic beauty.

The juxtaposition between life on and off the Kabuki stage is also rendered with precision through its visual language. On the stage, luminous lighting becomes a matter of elegance and grandeur. Offstage, natural lightings and restrained compositions create a contrast apart from the dialogue’s impacts.

‘Kokuho’ can also be claimed as the gateway to Japan’s theatrical heritage. Even without prior knowledge of Kabuki or the centuries-old tradition of onnagata, the film remains accessible. Each play is contextualised with its meaning being kept as a subtitle before its start. Therefore, rather than assuming familiarity, it immerses the audience in the art form’s rigorous discipline and cultural significance, resulting in the universality of the cultural specificity rather than making it alien.

As a film about theatrical acting, the heights it promises and sacrifices it demands, the cast leaves a remarkable legacy. Blending the technical precision of Kabuki with the psychological depiction exacted by a lifetime devoted to artistic perfection, the actors’ improvisations make the film particularly memorable.

We are initially told that Shunshuke is bound to carry his father’s legacy. Yet Kikuo's expertise unsettles that expectation. Crushed by the impossible weight of comparison and the fear of being eclipsed, Shunshuke’s, with his identity overlooked by his own father, withdraws out of inadequacy.

A scene where Shunshuke helps Kikuo apply his makeup backstage, ultimately leads to an imbalance between them, resulting in Kikuo’s emotional collapse. It is here that Kikuo confesses he wishes to drink a glass of Shunshuke’s blood. This startling expression of his desire to possess the effortless lineage and legitimacy that Shunshuke was born with, becomes one of the most emotionally daunting instances of the film.

“He is a national treasure. He will leave nothing but his art when he dies.”

The remark, made about Japan’s most celebrated Kabuki actor in his final moments, becomes Kikuo’s own aspiration, suggested by the film’s title ‘Kokuho’ which is translated as the ‘national treasure’.

Kabuki is an artform built upon the transformation of pain into beauty, and so is Kikuo’s life. Every moral compromise he embraces is transfigured into artistic brilliance on stage, making it an uneasy coexistence of empathy and moral dilemma for the audience.

Directed by: Sang-il Lee

Language: Japanese

Available on: Amazon Prime Video

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.

articles.title: Nepali workers among injured in Qatar gas plant explosion, 13 killed
articles.summary:
Nepali workers were among those injured in an explosion and fire at a gas processing facility in Qatar, authorities said, as officials confirmed that 13 people were killed and 66 were injured in one of the country’s deadliest industrial accidents in recent years.

The blast occurred on Sunday night at the Barzan gas processing facility inside the Ras Laffan Industrial City complex, according to Qatar Energy officials. The injured include workers from Nepal, Qatar, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Kenya, Ghana, Tanzania and Nigeria. Authorities said none of the injured is in a critical condition.

Energy minister and president and CEO of QatarEnergy, Saad bin Sherida al-Kaabi, said in Doha that the incident was a “technical accident” and not linked to sabotage or hostile activity. He said emergency teams and civil defence units brought the fire under control quickly.

Al-Kaabi said production at the Barzan facility had been halted for maintenance since December 2025 and was restarted only two days before the incident. He added that Qatar’s liquefied natural gas operations, export systems and port facilities were not affected.

The people killed were Indian and Pakistani nationals, he said.

Al-Kaabi said Qatar has sufficient gas reserves and alternative supply capacity, and the country’s export commitments will not be affected. He also expressed condolences to the families of the deceased and wished the injured a speedy recovery.

Authorities have launched an investigation into the cause of the explosion, Reuters reported.

Al-Kaabi said the incident is under review, while reiterating that there is no impact on wider energy infrastructure.

Qatar hosts one of the world’s largest liquefied natural gas export hubs at Ras Laffan.

articles.title: जापान भूकम्प : क्षतिग्रस्त एक भवनबाट २५ बिरालालाई उद्धार गरियो
articles.summary:
ठूलो भूकम्पपछि विस्फोटले ध्वस्त भएको जापानको एक सपिङ मलभित्र फसेका २५ बिरालालाई उद्धार गरिएको जापानी उद्धारकर्मीहरूले बिहीबार जनाएका छन्। यसले सामाजिक सञ्जालमा ठूलो प्रशंसासँगै राहतको लहर छाएको छ।

नर्वेली बिरालाहरू मोमो, कोहाकु, ताङ्गो, स्यान्डी अन्य बिरालाहरू मङ्गलबार ७.१ म्याग्निच्यूडको घातक भूकम्प जाँदा काशिमाको एओन मलको भुइँ तलामा रहेको क्याट क्याफे ‘मोफ्फ’मा थिए।

क्याफेका सञ्चालकहरूले भनेका छन्, 'मल खाली गरिएको थियो र कर्मचारीहरू बिरालाहरू लिन फर्किएका बेला ग्यासबाट हुनसक्ने ठूलो विस्फोटको हल्ला भवनभरि फैलियो। त्यसपछि कर्मचारीहरू भागे।'

अधिकारीहरूका अनुसार दक्षिणपश्चिमी कुमामोतो क्षेत्रका भूकम्पमा कम्तीमा ३४ जनाको मृत्यु भएको छ।

बुधबार दमकल सेवा, प्रहरी र मल सञ्चालकको अनुमति लिएर ‘मोफ्फ’का व्यवस्थापक भवनभित्र प्रवेश गरे र सबै २५ बिरालालाई सुरक्षित उद्धार गरे। बिरालाहरूलाई कुनै चोट लागेको थिएन। सोही दिन राति करिब १० बजे ती बिरालाहरूलाई जापानको पश्चिमी हिरोसिमा सहरमा सुरक्षित पुर्‍यायएको छ, त्यहाँ कम्पनीको अर्को क्याट क्याफे छ।

'कुमामोतोबाट लामो यात्राका कारण थकानको चिन्ता थियो, तर आइपुगेपछि हामीले प्रत्येकलाई व्यक्तिगत हेरचाह दियौँ,' क्याफे सञ्चालकले भने, 'अहिले बिरालाहरू ‘शान्त र स्थिर’ रूपमा समय बिताइरहेका छन्।'

‘लाइभडोर न्यूज’ ले सामाजिक सञ्जाल एक्समा पोस्ट गरेको बिरालाहरूको चमत्कारी उद्धारबारेको अनलाइन समाचार लेखलाई ७९ लाख व्यक्तिले हेरेका छन्।

एक प्रयोगकर्ताले इन्स्टाग्राममा लेखेका छन्, 'मानिसहरू भन्छन् कि मानवीय जीवन पहिले आउँछ, तर मानवीय जीवन र बिरालाको जीवन दुवै समान रूपमा मूल्यवान छन्। सबै सुरक्षित भएकोमा खुशी छु।'

जापानमा क्याट क्याफे, ‘हेजहग’ देखि साना सुँगुरसम्म पाल्तु जनावरहरूसँग खेल्न सकिने अन्य यस्तै प्रतिष्ठानहरू भने विवादास्पद छन्।

'सम्भव भएसम्म तिनीहरूलाई फेरि क्याट क्याफेमा नपठाई अपनाउने घरहरू खोजिदिनुहोस् जहाँ उनीहरू प्रेमले सुरक्षित र सुनिश्चित जीवन बाँच्न सकून्,' अर्का प्रयोगकर्ताले इन्स्टाग्राममा लेखेका छन्।

मलमा सात शव फेला परेको मानव क्षतिको सट्टा जनावरहरूमा मानिसहरूको ध्यान केन्द्रित भएको भन्दै पोष्टमा आलोचना पनि गरिएको छ। एएफपी

articles.title: देश छाड्न खोज्नेहरूको ताँती
articles.summary:
सरकारले स्वदेशमा भने जस्तो रोजगारीको वातावरण नबनाइदिएका कारण देश छाड्न खोज्नेहरूको ताँती झन् भयावह बनेको छ। दैनिक वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा झोला बोकेर जाने करिब दुई हजारको भिड, वैदेशिक रोजगार विभाग तथा कोरिया इपिएस शाखा, राहदानी विभाग लगायत सम्बन्धित सबै सरकारी कार्यालयमा पुगेर सेवा लिनेहरूको चाप विगतका वर्षमा भन्दा निकै बढेको छ।

बेलाबेलामा हुने त्रासदीपूर्ण राजनीतिक घटनाक्रम एवं विविध कारणले स्वदेशमा भएका उद्योग कलकारखाना एकपछि अर्को गर्दै धमाधम बन्द भएको, स्वरोजगार तथा साना उद्योग व्यवसाय सञ्चालनका लागि लगानीको वातावरण बिग्रनु र आर्थिक मन्दीको असरले स्वदेशमा काम नपाएर बाध्यताले देश छाडेर बिदेसिन खोज्नहरूको यस्तो लाइन लागेको हो।

विमानस्थलबाट अघिल्ला वर्षहरूमा दैनिक करिब एक हजार पाँच सयको संख्यामा मात्र विभिन्न मुलुकमा जाने गरेका थिए। अहिले देश छाडेर बिदेसिनेहरू पाँच सयभन्दा बढी छन्। युवा, श्रम तथा रोजगार मन्त्रालयअन्तर्गतको वैदेशिक रोजगार विभाग र परराष्ट्र मन्त्रालयले अध्यागमन कार्यालयको तथ् यांकलाई आधार बनाएर सार्वजनिक गरेको विवरणअनुसार अहिले हरेक दिन त्रिभुवन अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय विमानस्थलबाट दुई हजारको संख्यामा नेपाली बिदेसिएका छन्।

वैदेशिक रोजगार विभागका अनुसार गत आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ को ३२ असारसम्म कुल सात लाख ९२ हजार १ सय ८७ जना नेपाली कामदार श्रम स्वीकृति लिएर विभिन्न मुलुक गएका छन्। यसमध्ये पुरुष कामदारको संख्या ६ लाख ९७ हजार ९६ जना रहेको छ भने महिला कामदारको संख्या ९५ हजार ९१ जना रहेको छ।

अघिल्लो आव २०८१/८२ मा कुल ८ लाख ३९ हजार २ सय ६६ जना श्रम स्वीकृति लिएर बिदेसिएका थिए। अघिल्लो आवको तुलनामा यो संख्या (४७ हजार ७९ जना) ५.६ प्रतिशतले कमी हो। यस वर्ष सरकारले वैदेशिक रोजगारीका लागि कामदार पठाउन खुला गरेका १ सय १० देशमध्ये संयुक्त अरब इमिरेट्स (युएई) मा सबैभन्दा धेरै १ लाख ८३ हजार ५ सय ८० जना नेपाली कामदार श्रम स्वीकृति लिएर गएका छन्। अहिले मध्यपूर्वी क्षेत्रमा अमेरिका र इरानबिचको युद्धको त्रास जारी रहेका कारण अधिकांश नेपालीको रोजाइ दक्षिण कोरिया र युरोपियन श्रम गन्तव्य मुलुकतर्फ नै हुन थालेको छ।

दक्षिण कोरियामा जाने आकर्षण बढेसँगै काठमाडौंको त्रिपुरेश्वरस्थित राहदानी विभागमा देश छाडेर विभिन्न मुलुकमा जाने तयारीमा रहेकाहरूको लामै ताँती छ। बुधबार र बिहीबार अत्यधिक भीडमा देखिएको सो ताँती राहदानी बनाउनेको हो।

रोजगार अनुमति प्रणाली (इपिएस) मार्फत दक्षिण कोरियामा नेपाली कामदार पठाउन विगतका वर्षमा जस्तै सन् २०२६ का लागि कोरियामा जाने नेपाली कामदार छनोट गर्न गत सोमबारबाट कोरियन भाषा परीक्षाका लागि आवेदन खुला गरिएपछि काठमाडौंको त्रिपुरेश्वरस्थित राहदानी विभागमा पासपोर्ट लिन भिड लागेको छ। पासपोर्ट बनाउने लाइनमा युवायुवती बढी देखिन्छन्।

आगामी १७ साउनसम्म कोरियन भाषा परीक्षाका लागि आवेदन दिन पाइने भएका कारण इपिएसमार्फत दक्षिण कोरिया जान खोज्ने सेवाग्राहीको चाप बढेसँगै गत सातादेखि राहदानी विभागमा सेवाग्राहीको लामो ताँती लागिरहेको छ। यस्तो चापलाई मध्यनजर गर्दै राहदानी विभागले बिहीबारदेखि विद्युतीय राहदानीसम्बन्धी सेवा दुई सिफ्टमा सञ्चालन गर्न थालेको छ।

पछिल्लो समय सरकारले हालसम्मकै धेरै डाटा ट्रान्सफर गरेर नयाँ प्रणालीबाट ई–पासपोर्ट जारी गर्न सुरु गरेको र दैनिक १५ सय राहदानी छापिएको दाबी गरे पनि देश छाड्ने तयारीमा रहेका सेवाग्राही राहदानी लिन विभागमा पुग्दा घन्टौंसम्म लामो लाइनमा बसेर सास्ती भोग्न बाध्य छन्। सेवा सुधार्न सरकारले अनेक प्रयास गरेको दाबी गर्दै आए पनि अझै सेवाग्राहीले पाउने सास्ती उस्तै छ।

लामो समय लाइनमा बस्दा कहिले सर्भर डाउन भएको समस्या तथा कागजपत्रमा हस्ताक्षर गर्ने र प्रमाणित गर्ने हाकिम नभएको भन्दै विभागका कर्मचारीले विगतमा भन्दै आएको भनाइमा पनि कुनै परिवर्तन नदेखिएको अधिकांश सेवाग्राहीको गुनासो छ।

त्रिपुरेश्वरस्थित राहदानी विभागमा घन्टौं लाइन लागेर पनि बिहीबार राहदानी बनाउन नपाएका नुवाकोटका सेवाग्राही रामकृष्ण श्रेष्ठले सरकारले राम्रो सेवा दिएको दाबी गरे पनि अझै सेवा लिन विगतमा भोग्दै आएको बाध्यता नहटेको गुनासो गरे। यसअघि तीन वर्ष कतारको वैदेशिक रोजगारीबाट फर्किएर म्याद सकिएको राहदानी बनाएर अब दक्षिण कोरिया जाने तयारीमा रहेका श्रेष्ठले नागरिक दैनिकसँग भने, ‘यहाँ घन्टौंसम्म कुर्नुपर्ने, पटकपटक सर्भर प्रणाली अवरुद्ध हुने, अनलाइन भुक्तानी स्वीकार नहुने, अपोइन्टमेन्ट छिटै बन्द भइहाल्ने तथा राहदानी वितरणमा ढिलाइ हुने समस्या सेवाग्राहीले भोगिरहेका छन्।’

दिनभर लाइनमा बसेर पनि आफ्नो काम नसकिएको आक्रोश पोख्दै श्रेष्ठले भने, ‘आफूले खोजेको मितिमा अपोइन्टमेन्ट पनि नपाइने यो कस्तो सेवा हो ? अर्का सेवाग्राही रामेछापका हिक्मत कार्कीले पनि विगत दुई/तीन दिनदेखि आफूले राहदानी बनाउन दिनभर लाइनमा पसेर पालो कुर्दै बस्दा अझै काम नसकिने हो कि ? भन्ने निश्चित नभएको बताए। श्रेष्ठ र कार्की त प्रतिनिधि पात्र मात्र हुन्। अहिले राहदानी विभागमा पुगेर दिनभर लाइनमा बसेर पनि समयमा काम नभएपछि धेरैले यस्तो समस्याबारे जानकारी गराएका छन्।

सन् २०१८ देखि फ्रान्सेली कम्पनी आइडिमियाले सञ्चालन गर्दै आएको राहदानी छपाइ तथा व्यवस्थापनको जिम्मेवारी अहिले सरकारले जर्मन कम्पनी ‘म्युहलबउर’ र ‘भेरिडोस’ लाई हस्तान्तरण गरेको छ। कम्पनी परिवर्तन गर्दा सरकारले पहिलेको प्रणालीभन्दा अझ आधुनिक, गुणस्तरीय, छिटो र सर्वसुलभ सेवा दिने लक्ष्यसहित पुरानो ठेक्का अन्त्य गरेर नयाँ ई–पासपोर्ट प्रणाली लागु गरेको दाबी गरेको थियो, तर व्यवहारमा भने अपेक्षाअनुसार काम हुन नसकेको सेवाग्राहीको आरोप छ।

लाइनमा बसेका अधिकांश सेवाग्राहीका अनुसार सबै प्रक्रिया पु¥याएर आवेदन दिँदा राहदानी लिन झन्डै दुई साताको समय पाउने अवस्था छ। सरकारको यस्तो काम गर्ने तरिकाबाट सेवाग्राहीले सास्ती भोग्नुपरेको उनको भनाइ छ। कोरियन भाषा परीक्षामा सहभागी हुन आवेदन दिने सेवाग्राहीको चाप बढेसँगै राहदानी विभागले पनि बिहीबारबाट विद्युतीय राहदानी सेवा दुई सिफ्टमा सञ्चालन गरेको छ।

राहदानी विभागले आगामी २२ साउनसम्म विद्युतीय राहदानीसम्बन्धी सेवा दुई सिफ्टमा सञ्चालन गरिने बताएको छ। विभागले सार्वजनिक बिदाको दिनमा समेत राहदानी सेवा प्रदान गर्ने निणर्य गरेको जनाएको छ। विभागका अनुसार राहदानी वितरण कार्य पहिलो सिफ्ट बिहान ७ देखि २ बजे र दोस्रो सिफ्ट दिउँसो २ देखि राती ९ बजेसम्म सञ्चालन हुनेछ। विभागले सेवाग्राहीको सहजताका लागि शनिबार र सार्वजनिक बिदाका दिनसमेत बिहान १० देखि बेलुकी ४ बजेसम्म राहदानी सेवा उपलब्ध गराउने जनाएको छ।

इपिएस कोरिया शाखाले यस वर्ष कुल सात हजार २ सय जना नेपाली कामदार पठाउन भाषा परीक्षाको आवेदन खुलाएपछि अहिले वैदेशिक रोजगारीको आकर्षक श्रम गन्तव्य मूलुक दक्षिण कोरिया जाने तयारीमा रहेका युवाको चाप बढेको हो।

पछिल्लो एक सातादेखि विशेषगरी दक्षिण कोरिया जानका लागि लिइने इपिएस भाषा परीक्षाका लागि आवेदन दिने सेवाग्राहीको संख्या बढेको छ। सोही कारण राहदानी विभागमा पुगेर राहदानी लिने सेवाग्राहीलाई सहजरूपमा सेवा उपलब्ध गराउन यस्तो व्यवस्था गरिएको विभागले जनाएको छ।

यसैगरी शनिबार र आइतबारको सार्वजनिक बिदाको दिनसमेत विभागले विद्युतीय राहदानीसम्बन्धी सेवा सञ्चालन गर्ने जनाएको छ। अहिले इपिएस भाषा परीक्षाका लागि आवेदन दिने सेवाग्राहीको संख्या बढेसँगै राहदानी बनाउन आउनेको चापसमेत बढेको हो। कोरिया रोजगारीका लागि आवश्यक प्रक्रिया अघि बढाउन राहदानी अनिवार्य हुने भएकाले पछिल्लो एक सातादेखि राहदानी लिन सेवाग्राहीको चाप बढेको विभागले जनाएको छ।

सेवाग्राहीको बढ्दो चापलाई व्यवस्थापन गर्दै समयमै सेवा उपलब्ध गराउने उद्देश्यले अतिरिक्त समय र दुई सिफ्टमा सेवा सञ्चालनको व्यवस्था गरिएकाले अब विस्तारै चप कम हुने विभागले जनाएको छ।

articles.title: शुद्धोधन गाउँपालिकाका उपाध्यक्षसहित दुई जनाविरुद्ध भ्रष्टाचार मुद्दा
articles.summary:
अख्तियार दुरुपयोग अनुसन्धान आयोगले कपिलवस्तुको शुद्धोधन गाउँपालिकाका उपाध्यक्ष होमप्रकाश चौधरी कुर्मी र गाउँपालिकाका तत्कालीन ‘एमआइएस अपरेटर’ सुरेश कँहारविरुद्ध विशेष अदालतमा भ्रष्टाचार मुद्दा दायर गरेको छ।

आयोगका अनुसार गाउँपालिकामा जागिर लगाइदिने भन्दै घुस लिएको भन्ने उजुरीमाथि अनुसन्धान गर्दा उपाध्यक्ष चौधरीको बैंक खातामा रु पाँच लाख जम्मा भएको पुष्टि भएपछि आज विशेष अदालत काठमाडौंमा आरोपपत्र दायर गरिएको हो।

अनुसन्धानका क्रममा आर्थिक वर्ष २०७९/८० को स्वीकृत वार्षिक कार्यक्रमअन्तर्गत सञ्चालन हुने ‘न्यायिक असमानताविरुद्ध उपाध्यक्ष कार्यक्रम’ सञ्चालन गर्ने जिम्मेवारी तत्कालीन एमआइएस अपरेटर कँहारलाई दिइएको थियो। सो कार्यक्रम सञ्चालनका लागि गाउँपालिकासँग सम्झौता गरी रु छ लाख पेश्की लिएको र उक्त रकम खातामा आएलगत्तै त्यसमध्ये रु पाँच लाख उपाध्यक्ष चौधरीको बैंक खातामा जम्मा गरिएको आयोगले जनाएको छ।

लिइएको पेश्की रकमबाट तोकिएको कार्यक्रममा खर्च नगरी घुस र रिसवतका रूपमा उपाध्यक्ष चौधरीलाई उपलब्ध गराइएको आरोप लागेको छ। सो कार्यमा उपाध्यक्ष चौधरी र तत्कालीन एमआइएस अपरेटर कँहारबीच मिलेमतो रहेको अनुसन्धानबाट खुलेको छ।

आयोगले उनीहरू विरुद्ध रु पाँच लाख बिगो कायम गरी कैद, बिगोबमोजिम जरिवाना तथा घुसस्वरुप लिइएको रकम जफतको मागदाबीसहित विशेष अदालतमा मुद्दा दायर गरिएको जनाएको छ।

articles.title: सामाजिक सञ्जालमा भ्रामक सूचना फैलाउने युवक सर्लाही प्रहरीको नियन्त्रणमा
articles.summary:
सामाजिक सञ्जाल फेसबुकमार्फत सार्वजनिक शान्ति, सुरक्षा तथा सामाजिक सद्भावमा प्रतिकूल असर पर्ने प्रकृतिका भ्रामक तथा झुटा सूचना प्रसारण गरेको आरोपमा सर्लाही प्रहरीले एक युवकलाई नियन्त्रणमा लिएको छ।

जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालय सर्लाहीले शुक्रबार जारी गरेको प्रेस विज्ञप्तिअनुसार फेसबुक प्रोफाइल 'मुकेश कुमार यादव समर्थक' नामबाट भ्रामक भिडियो तथा समाचार सार्वजनिक गरेको सूचनापछि प्रहरीले अनुसन्धान थालेको थियो।

अनुसन्धानका क्रममा उक्त फेसबुक आईडी सञ्चालन गर्ने व्यक्ति सर्लाहीको धनकौल गाउँपालिका–२ निवासी ३० वर्षीय राम प्रवेश राय यादव रहेको खुलेको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ। उनलाई नियन्त्रणमा लिई प्रयोग गरेको मोबाइलसमेत बरामद गरेको हो।

सोधपुछका क्रममा उनले आफ्नै फेसबुक आईडीमार्फत उक्त भ्रामक भिडियो तथा सूचना प्रसारण गरेको प्रहरी समक्ष स्वीकार गरेका छन्। यस्ता सामग्री सामाजिक सञ्जालमा प्रकाशन तथा प्रसारण गरी सर्वसाधारणमा भ्रम सिर्जना गर्ने, सार्वजनिक शान्ति–सुरक्षा तथा सुव्यवस्थामा प्रतिकूल असर पार्ने कार्य गरेको आरोपमा उनीमाथि विद्युतीय कारोबार ऐन अन्तर्गत पाँच दिनको म्याद थप गरी थप अनुसन्धान भइरहेको जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालय सर्लाहीले जनाएको छ।

प्रहरीले सामाजिक सञ्जाल प्रयोग गर्दा अपुष्ट, झुटा वा भ्रामक सूचना साझा नगर्न तथा जिम्मेवार ढंगले डिजिटल माध्यमको प्रयोग गर्न सर्वसाधारणलाई आग्रह गरेको छ।

articles.title: जापान भूकम्प : क्षतिग्रस्त एक भवनबाट २५ बिरालालाई उद्धार गरियो
articles.summary:
ठूलो भूकम्पपछि विस्फोटले ध्वस्त भएको जापानको एक सपिङ मलभित्र फसेका २५ बिरालालाई उद्धार गरिएको जापानी उद्धारकर्मीहरूले बिहीबार जनाएका छन्। यसले सामाजिक सञ्जालमा ठूलो प्रशंसासँगै राहतको लहर छाएको छ।

नर्वेली बिरालाहरू मोमो, कोहाकु, ताङ्गो, स्यान्डी अन्य बिरालाहरू मङ्गलबार ७.१ म्याग्निच्यूडको घातक भूकम्प जाँदा काशिमाको एओन मलको भुइँ तलामा रहेको क्याट क्याफे ‘मोफ्फ’मा थिए।

क्याफेका सञ्चालकहरूले भनेका छन्, 'मल खाली गरिएको थियो र कर्मचारीहरू बिरालाहरू लिन फर्किएका बेला ग्यासबाट हुनसक्ने ठूलो विस्फोटको हल्ला भवनभरि फैलियो। त्यसपछि कर्मचारीहरू भागे।'

अधिकारीहरूका अनुसार दक्षिणपश्चिमी कुमामोतो क्षेत्रका भूकम्पमा कम्तीमा ३४ जनाको मृत्यु भएको छ।

बुधबार दमकल सेवा, प्रहरी र मल सञ्चालकको अनुमति लिएर ‘मोफ्फ’का व्यवस्थापक भवनभित्र प्रवेश गरे र सबै २५ बिरालालाई सुरक्षित उद्धार गरे। बिरालाहरूलाई कुनै चोट लागेको थिएन। सोही दिन राति करिब १० बजे ती बिरालाहरूलाई जापानको पश्चिमी हिरोसिमा सहरमा सुरक्षित पुर्‍यायएको छ, त्यहाँ कम्पनीको अर्को क्याट क्याफे छ।

'कुमामोतोबाट लामो यात्राका कारण थकानको चिन्ता थियो, तर आइपुगेपछि हामीले प्रत्येकलाई व्यक्तिगत हेरचाह दियौँ,' क्याफे सञ्चालकले भने, 'अहिले बिरालाहरू ‘शान्त र स्थिर’ रूपमा समय बिताइरहेका छन्।'

‘लाइभडोर न्यूज’ ले सामाजिक सञ्जाल एक्समा पोस्ट गरेको बिरालाहरूको चमत्कारी उद्धारबारेको अनलाइन समाचार लेखलाई ७९ लाख व्यक्तिले हेरेका छन्।

एक प्रयोगकर्ताले इन्स्टाग्राममा लेखेका छन्, 'मानिसहरू भन्छन् कि मानवीय जीवन पहिले आउँछ, तर मानवीय जीवन र बिरालाको जीवन दुवै समान रूपमा मूल्यवान छन्। सबै सुरक्षित भएकोमा खुशी छु।'

जापानमा क्याट क्याफे, ‘हेजहग’ देखि साना सुँगुरसम्म पाल्तु जनावरहरूसँग खेल्न सकिने अन्य यस्तै प्रतिष्ठानहरू भने विवादास्पद छन्।
